We ended our study of Ibn Sīnā by trying to draw a general conclusion about the tendencies that define the overall direction of his philosophy.

This conclusion brings together both his materialist and his idealist positions and traces each of them back to its intellectual, ideological, and social foundations.

Our final judgment was that Ibn Sīnā cannot be regarded as a completely materialist philosopher, because the idealist elements in his system are not merely marginal.

But we can say that the general direction of his thought is materialist, and that its central starting points are materialist.

PreviousThe Problem of Existence and Essence in Ibn Sīnā’s PhilosophyNextConclusion

Conclusion

1

Ibn Sīnā’s philosophy marked the culmination of the stages through which Arab philosophical thought had developed from the eighth century to the first third of the eleventh—a period of roughly three centuries. This was a short span compared with the much longer histories of the Eastern and Western, especially Greek, philosophical traditions that came before it.

Yet despite this relatively short period, the conditions of Arab-Islamic society allowed Arab philosophy to play two important roles in the history of world philosophy.

First, it brought Greek philosophy back to life after it had become scattered, fragmented, and confined for several generations to a number of monasteries and Nestorian, Jacobite, and Persian schools in the East, such as those of Edessa, Nisibis, Harran, and Jundishapur.

Second, Arab philosophy left its mark on part of medieval European philosophy through what it had achieved in the study of nature. Historically, serious discussion of nature in Europe, and attempts to understand what nature itself was, began only after Europeans became familiar with the philosophy of Ibn Sīnā. As his name spread among medieval European philosophers, they began discussing such questions as the division of natural things into living and non-living forms, movement in nature, and other problems of this kind.

2

This double historical role of Arab philosophy raises two main questions for any scientific understanding of the history of philosophy.

The first is how Greek philosophy was brought back to life during the age of Arab philosophy.

The second is how Arab philosophy, in turn, influenced medieval European philosophy.

On the first question, we need to stress something we have tried to show throughout this book. When Greek philosophy, in both its Athenian and Alexandrian forms, came to life again in the philosophical work of Arab thinkers, it did so in a social, intellectual, and ideological setting that was fundamentally different from the one in which Greek philosophy had originally appeared and developed.

The main reason was the difference between the social relations of the ancient Greek and Roman worlds and those of medieval Arab-Islamic society.

Ancient Greek and Roman society was based on slavery. Society was divided mainly between two classes: slave-owning masters and slaves.

Arab-Islamic society, by contrast, was based mainly on feudal relations of production. Alongside these were relatively developed forms of trade and banking, which had become an integral part of the society’s economic and social structure.

This fundamental difference necessarily changed the basis on which classes were formed. It also greatly widened the range of people who could take part in cultural life.

In slave-owning Greek society, slaves and some groups among the so-called “free” population were completely excluded from cultural activity and had no right to take part in it. Cultural life was largely restricted to the upper layers of the free population.

In medieval Arab-Islamic society, the situation was very different.

The kind of practical social activity people perform is one of the factors that shapes cultural activity, both in the forms it takes and in the kinds of people who take part in it.

It was therefore natural that Arab-Islamic society should differ from ancient Greek society not only in the groups of people producing culture, but also in the culture they produced. This difference necessarily appeared in the ideological sphere as well. Intellectual activity, like social and political activity, always has a class character, and philosophy is one of the highest forms of intellectual activity.

The history of knowledge in ancient Greece itself confirms this close and objective connection between practical social life and intellectual activity.

Why, for example, was Greek philosophy so closely connected with the study of nature?

The reason is that the earliest Greek philosophers were also engaged in practical life. Some were sailors, merchants, or politicians. Their theoretical ideas were therefore closely connected with, and shaped by, their practical activity.

That is why philosophical knowledge did not first appear in ancient Greece as philosophy in a narrow sense. It began as knowledge about nature. Only later was that knowledge organized into philosophical theories and hypotheses.

Given the deep difference between the ancient Greek-Roman world on the one hand and medieval Arab-Islamic society on the other, it would have been completely unnatural and unrealistic for Arab philosophy to take over Greek philosophy with exactly the same meanings and content it had possessed in a slave-owning society.

The old forms of production had disappeared. New forms had taken their place, together with new historical forms of knowledge and new ways of understanding the world.

We should also remember that Greek philosophy was not the only source of Arab-Islamic philosophy.

Its sources were many and varied.

One was Islam itself—as religion, thought, law, and ideology. Islam formed the theoretical climate in which Arab-Islamic philosophy grew and was shaped.

Other sources included the ancient and contemporary philosophical traditions of the East: Persian and Indian thought, as well as the older traditions of Mesopotamia, Egypt, and Syria.

These sources were historically and socially connected with Arab-Islamic philosophy even more deeply than Greek philosophy was.

This makes it even clearer that Greek philosophy could not simply enter Arab-Islamic thought unchanged. Its philosophical meanings and content had to be altered, and so did its ideological content.

The ideology of a pagan slave-owning society could not simply remain the same when it entered an Islamic society based on feudalism and trade—a society that was far more varied and complex in its economic, social, political, and cultural structure, especially in its class composition. Cultural activity itself also rested on a much broader social base, with new classes and groups taking part in it.

This was one of the most important questions we tried to study carefully in this book.

Our purpose was not simply to argue against bourgeois and Orientalist views of Arab philosophy and of the Arab intellectual heritage in general.

More importantly, we wanted to show the deep connection between that heritage and the historical development of Arab-Islamic society over roughly four centuries of the Middle Ages.

We also wanted to uncover the materialist tendencies and positions that appeared within Arab-Islamic philosophy through an internal struggle with idealist tendencies and positions. These included the idealism found even in Greek philosophy up to Aristotle, as well as the much clearer idealism of Plato and Neoplatonism.

We discussed this question at length in the introduction to the first volume.

The second question is the influence of Arab-Islamic philosophy on medieval European philosophy. This needs some further explanation here, because it helps show the active historical role Arab philosophy played in the development of world philosophical thought.

We should begin with a historical fact that helped make this influence possible.

During the Middle Ages, an Arab state arose within which a number of different states later developed. Despite their differences, they remained culturally connected, at least, with the Islamic caliphate in the East, whose centers shifted between Syria, Iraq, and Egypt.

These states spread across countries with different peoples, histories, civilizations, and cultures. They also extended across different geographical regions in all three continents: Asia, Africa, and Europe.

This was the external historical factor we referred to earlier. It created the conditions for many different cultures to become absorbed into Arab culture.

The same situation later helped this many-sided Arab culture come into contact with European culture.

That exchange could have been much broader and deeper if Arab culture had been able to continue developing creatively for a longer historical period. It could also have gone further if Arab thinkers had studied the other emerging European cultures of the Middle Ages as closely as they studied one European culture in particular: ancient Greek culture.

But that is not what happened.

Instead, medieval European culture took the initiative in studying Arab culture. The relationship between the two therefore became largely one-sided. For that reason, the influence during the Middle Ages was also largely one-sided.

Before looking at concrete examples of Arab philosophy’s influence on medieval Europe, we need to understand the social differences reflected in the two philosophical traditions.

When we speak of “medieval philosophy,” we are speaking, first, of the philosophy of European feudal society and, second, of the philosophy of Arab-Islamic feudal society.

Both had feudal relations of production as their social base. In that sense, they belonged to the same broad type of social system.

But European feudalism was different from feudalism in the East.

This was a historical difference that the founders of Marxism, Marx and Engels, themselves took into account when they used their well-known term, the “Asiatic mode of production.”

The difference was clearly reflected in philosophy.

One important historical sign of it can be seen in what happened after the collapse of the centralized Roman Empire.

Europe broke up into principalities. Wars then broke out among them as larger feudal powers tried to gather smaller principalities around themselves.

Out of this process came the gradual formation of the European nations, a process that continued throughout the Middle Ages and was not completed until the nineteenth century.

During this long period, the Vatican was the only major center of unity in Europe.

It therefore developed into a state that exercised authority over Europe’s feudal powers while still retaining its Christian religious character.

Within the Arab-Islamic Empire, the situation was different.

The caliphate ruled as both religious and civil authority. There were not two separate powers. The caliphal state represented the feudal social order as a whole.

Later, when relatively independent principalities and small states began to appear inside the caliphate, the centralized feudal order began to break apart.

At the same time, the feudal structure became increasingly military in character. This deepened its weakness, held back rural production, and exhausted the productive forces of the countryside.

As a result, the main forms of production increasingly overlapped, and the boundaries between them became unclear. It became difficult to say whether the economy was mainly rural, craft-based, commercial, or all of these at once.

3

These two different historical situations were reflected in philosophy in different ways.

In Europe, philosophy took an almost entirely theological direction and revolved around one central question: God.

During the Middle Ages, philosophical thought was largely confined to questions about the relationship between God, Christ, and Mary, together with the question of how God created the world.

The doctrine that God created the world from nothing became dominant, along with the doctrine of the Trinity and the idea of original sin.

The Vatican drew part of its authority from these three doctrines.

In the Islamic East, the situation was different.

In content, philosophical thought turned toward the human being and nature. In form, it still expressed itself in terms of God.

From the very beginning of philosophical thought in Arab-Islamic history, the human being was one of its central concerns.

The Qadarites raised the issue first, followed by the Muʿtazilites. They emphasized human freedom of choice and human responsibility for action.

Against them stood the Jabrites, whose doctrine of predestination gave ideological expression to a ruling power that presented its authority as the expression of divine will and therefore as a fate people had no choice but to accept.

This question of the human being remained one of the basic themes of Arab-Islamic philosophy all the way to Ibn Rushd, where it reached its highest development.

The question of nature also became central because the development of society itself created a need to study it.

During the early period of the centralized Abbasid caliphate, wide possibilities opened up for the growth of the economy, science, and philosophical thought.

At the same time, early ideological struggles under a centralized system of absolute and authoritarian rule often took place in the language of Islamic theology.

But there is another important feature here.

Most of the thinkers who built the early movement of philosophical thought came from the middle social groups, especially from people connected with trades and professions. We can see this even in names such as al-Naẓẓām, al-ʿAllāf, al-Khayyāṭ, al-ʿAṭṭār, and al-Ghazālī.

Many of these thinkers were also of non-Arab origin, and under Umayyad rule the political authorities often looked down on people from such backgrounds.

All of this helped give philosophical thought, from an early stage, an ideological direction that stood in opposition to the ideology of the existing state.

These were among the factors that helped produce materialist tendencies within Arab philosophy, in forms shaped by their own particular historical conditions.

4

It is not by accident that historians of medieval European philosophy mark the end of its first stage and the beginning of its second around the time Europeans first became familiar with Arab philosophy.

This shows how important that historical encounter was for the development of European philosophy.

It helped produce a major shift in direction.

European philosophy moved from what is usually called its patristic period, the age of the Church Fathers, which reached its end with Saint Augustine, into what historians have called the period of Arab and Jewish philosophical influence.

At that time, economic development in the Arab world was far ahead of Europe.

There was hardly any comparison.

Much of Europe was still dominated by the remains of a largely self-sufficient local economy within feudal principalities.

In the Arab world, by contrast, a market and money economy was developing and flourishing. It was opening foreign markets even in distant regions such as Russia and had begun reaching as far as Scandinavia.

During this period, Europe produced few philosophers in the strict sense of the word until the appearance of Thomas Aquinas, who lived from 1225 to 1274. By then, the great period of Arab philosophy had already come to an end.

Aquinas’s philosophy showed a much stronger interest in nature, and here he was influenced by Arab philosophy, whose influence was spreading among European thinkers.

The names of Arab scientists such as Jābir ibn Ḥayyān, al-Ḥasan ibn al-Haytham, al-Khwārizmī, and Ibn Sīnā were becoming increasingly well known in these circles.

European thinkers began to feel a need to study their achievements in astronomy, chemistry, medicine, anatomy, and mathematics, even though popular hostility toward Arabs and Jews was widespread in Europe at the time.

5

As we have already argued, the rise of materialist tendencies in Arab philosophy was closely connected with economic development in the Arab world.

That economic development created the original drive toward scientific and technical achievements in the natural sciences and mathematics, which were still considered part of philosophy.

From this point of view, the entry of Arab philosophy into European intellectual history, and the influence it had on European philosophy, also helped open European philosophy toward the study of nature.

This was one of the first paths through which European philosophy began moving toward materialist tendencies.

Early signs of this change appeared in debates over the creation of the world.

Before Europe came into contact with Arab philosophy, the dominant doctrine held that the world had been created from nothing.

Later, the views of Arab philosophers such as al-Fārābī, Ibn Sīnā, Ibn Rushd, and others began to spread among European philosophers. These views rejected the idea of creation from nothing.

From the time Europeans became familiar with Ibn Sīnā’s philosophy, they continued drawing on his ideas about nature and the creation of the world until roughly the eighteenth century.

We have already mentioned his influence in encouraging European philosophers to discuss such questions as the division of nature into living and non-living forms, natural motion, and other problems concerning the material world outside the mind.

6

Medieval European scholastic philosophy developed teachings about different forms of essence and often explained them in extremely simple and superficial ways.

For example, scholastic thinkers might say that a clock shows the time because it contains an invisible inner power that makes it do so.

They might explain the fact that a flea can jump a distance greater than its own size by appealing to its essential form: the flea’s essence, they argued, contains the power that allows it to jump so far.

Ibn Sīnā’s physics was far more advanced than explanations of this kind.

He tried to understand natural phenomena through the phenomena themselves—that is, through their own laws.

Both he and Ibn Rushd, for example, studied the nature of heat, cold, moisture, dryness, and vapor, as well as the workings of hearing, sight, and other natural processes.

This way of approaching nature as a subject for scientific study reached Europe before the European Renaissance.

Through Arab philosophy, especially the work of Ibn Sīnā and Ibn Rushd, the idea of “double truth”590 also entered medieval European philosophy: the idea that there is a philosophical truth and a religious truth.

In reality, however, the Arab philosophers did not truly believe there were two separate truths. According to our interpretation, this apparent division was a mask that allowed them to conceal their belief that philosophical truth was ultimately one.

The spread of the teachings of Ibn Sīnā and Ibn Rushd in medieval Europe also gave logic a much more important place.

This influence appeared clearly in European scholastic debates over the relationship between the universal and the individual.

Ibn Sīnā described this relationship in three different ways, all of which later appeared in scholastic philosophy: the universal exists before things, within things, and after things.

Before its encounter with Arab philosophy, the medieval European Church recognized only the Bible as a source for knowledge of God.

After that encounter, it also came to recognize Aristotle as another path toward such knowledge.

We have already mentioned one historical example of this influence.

Thomas Aquinas studied Ibn Sīnā and Ibn Rushd for many years. Through them, he also became familiar with Aristotle by reading Arabic translations of Aristotelian philosophy, since Aquinas knew Arabic.

Arab philosophy continued to influence thinkers of the European Renaissance.

Ideas found in Ibn Sīnā and Ibn Rushd—such as the eternity of matter, its circular motion, and the transformation of forms while matter itself remains—later appeared as accepted ideas in thinkers such as Giordano Bruno, who lived from 1548 to 1600.

They also appeared in Pietro Pomponazzi, who lived from 1464 to 1524 and was executed on charges of promoting atheism because he was regarded as an Averroist.

Another Italian philosopher, Bernardino Telesio, who lived from 1508 to 1588, adopted Ibn Rushd’s theory that heat is what causes non-living matter to pass into life.

Finally, we need only look at the philosophical schools that arose in Europe either in support of Averroist philosophy or in opposition to it.

Their very existence is clear evidence of the important historical role Arab philosophy played in the development of materialist tendencies—not only in the East, but in the West as well.

Materialist philosophy continued to develop from there until the eventual appearance of dialectical materialism.

7

Arab philosophy entered ideological struggle from the very beginning of its formation.

It first appeared through the ideas of the group known as the Qadarites. They rejected the idea that human beings were helpless before fate, while also rejecting the rule of an absolute and authoritarian political system that justified itself in the name of divine destiny.

The Muʿtazilites later continued along the path opened by the Qadarites.

As philosophical thought developed into more complete systems in the work of al-Kindī, al-Fārābī, Abū Bakr al-Rāzī, Ibn Sīnā, and eventually Ibn Rushd, the ideological struggle also rose to a higher level.

This happened alongside the growth of class conflict, which became sharper as social divisions increased along both class and ethnic lines in a society whose economy was developing at different rates under different historical conditions.

Arab philosophy later continued this struggle even after it had left its original historical environment in the Arab-Islamic lands and entered medieval Europe.

There, it helped the growing progressive forces within medieval, and later modern, European philosophy move toward materialist philosophical positions.

These positions became one of the main fronts of ideological struggle in Europe between Christian theology and science.

In our own time, Arab philosophy has once again entered this field of struggle, though now in a new and modern form.

The conflict today is between the forces of the reactionary Arab bourgeoisie, allied with and dependent on world imperialism, and the national and progressive forces fighting for national liberation and social progress.

Culture in all its forms—literature, art, philosophy, and the other human sciences—has become one of the main fields in which this struggle takes place.

As a result, cultural class struggle has become increasingly important within the wider struggle for national and social liberation, and the role played by revolutionary intellectuals has become broader and more influential.

It is in this same context that a new question has emerged: how should we deal with our national cultural heritage from an ideological point of view?

The heritage itself has become an intellectual weapon used by each side in a struggle being fought on many fronts, both intellectual and social.

Historically, general interest in the Arab cultural heritage goes back to the early period of what is usually called the Arab Renaissance, or Nahḍa.

This period began around the middle of the nineteenth century.

At that time, most Arab countries were under the rule of the Ottoman Turkish Empire. Some, such as Egypt, were under British military occupation. Others, such as Algeria, were being subjected by French colonialism and occupation to attempts to erase their national identity.

Under these conditions, interest in Arab cultural heritage became one means of resisting foreign rulers and occupiers.

By teaching the Arab public about the historical achievements of earlier generations, intellectuals hoped to awaken a sense of national identity and a desire for liberation.

A generation of intellectuals appeared in Egypt, Lebanon, Syria, and Iraq.

Among them were Muslim religious thinkers such as Muḥammad ʿAbduh in Egypt, ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Kawākibī in Syria, and Maḥmūd Shukrī al-Ālūsī in Iraq.

There were also Christian and Muslim Lebanese thinkers such as Buṭrus al-Bustānī, Nāṣīf al-Yāzijī, and Aḥmad Fāris al-Shidyāq.

Later generations of Arab intellectuals continued to show growing interest in the national cultural heritage, though in new forms.

They used it to strengthen national feeling, encourage resistance to colonial rule, and help build an Arab public opinion that demanded independence for the Arab countries still under the Ottoman caliphate.

After the First World War, these countries separated from Turkey.

Some then came under French mandate rule, including Syria and Lebanon.

Palestine came under British mandate rule.

Iraq gained only a formal kind of political independence.

Egypt remained under British occupation.

The countries of North Africa—Tunisia, Algeria, and Morocco—remained under French control, while Libya remained under Italian occupation.

Under these conditions, interest in the cultural heritage kept its role as part of the struggle for liberation.

During these periods of resistance, interest in the heritage increasingly took the form of publishing old works and writing studies about them.

In that sense, the approach became more systematic and rational.

Arab intellectuals studying in Western European universities also began using bourgeois methods of research to study their national cultural heritage.

But throughout all the earlier stages we have described, the relationship with the heritage was still shaped by a basic assumption: the past was surrounded by a kind of sacred halo simply because it was the past.

It was praised for its own sake.

Any critical re-examination of one part of the heritage or another could be condemned as a national or religious form of heresy.

Certain areas of the heritage were treated as forbidden territory, with a clear red line placed in front of scientific research.

After the Second World War, the method of studying the heritage began to change.

National liberation movements had started to win important victories.

Popular movements were spreading and taking a larger role in struggles for liberation.

Arab forces of liberation and progress were also coming into closer contact with revolutionary movements elsewhere in the world, especially after the democratic alliance decisively defeated the Nazi and fascist Axis powers at the end of the war.

Under these conditions, and especially from the 1940s onward, attitudes toward the national cultural heritage increasingly became part of a much sharper and deeper ideological struggle.

Positions toward the heritage now divided along these lines.

Bourgeois and right-wing thought turned toward the idealist and supernatural sides of the heritage.

Progressive thought, by contrast, turned to the heritage in order to uncover its real historical foundations and to see all its different sides, both positive and negative.

This book itself was written as a serious contribution to building an understanding of our heritage that can strengthen the fighting spirit of our people in their struggle for national and social liberation across the Arab world.

It was also written as an intellectual weapon against a reactionary effort that has been taking place for a long time in the field of Arab intellectual heritage.

The aim of that effort has been to hide the heritage’s real historical character and, by doing so, to keep the present tied to the backward thought of our distant past.

8

The research in this book stops with Ibn Sīnā, whom we have treated as marking the end of the mature stage of Arab-Islamic philosophy in the East.

About a century after Ibn Sīnā, Arab-Islamic philosophy resumed its great struggle in the Maghreb against the reactionary intellectual repression whose banner al-Ghazālī had carried for several generations.

That struggle found its strongest expression in the philosophy of Ibn Rushd and in the progressive Averroist current that grew around it.

The author of this book will continue his study of this final stage of Arab-Islamic philosophy once the work required for the present part of the book has been completed.

  • Husayn Muruwwa was born in 1910, according to his official papers, though he himself believed that he was probably born in 1908. He was born in the village of Hadatha, in the Bint Jbeil district of southern Lebanon. He received his early education in Bint Jbeil and Nabatieh.

  • In 1924, he travelled to Iraq to study religious sciences, Arabic language, and Arabic literature at the religious college in Najaf. He completed his studies there in 1938.

  • In 1948, he took an active part—as a political participant, journalist, and writer—in Iraq’s national popular uprising known as the Wathba, which brought down the colonial British Portsmouth Treaty with the Iraqi monarchy. After the conservative reaction that followed, Nuri al-Said—described here as “Britain’s man in Iraq”—returned to power. In May 1949, he ordered Husayn Muruwwa to be expelled from Iraq. Muruwwa returned to Lebanon in June of that year.

  • Back in Lebanon, he began writing his well-known daily column, “With the Caravan,” for the newspaper al-Hayat. He also helped found the left-wing magazine al-Thaqafa al-Wataniyya and worked on its editorial staff from 1952 until it ceased publication as a literary and intellectual magazine in 1959. From the 1950s onward, he also contributed to the magazine al-Tariq, and from the late 1960s until the day of his assassination he oversaw its editorial work. He also wrote for the newspapers al-Nidaʾ and al-Akhbar.

  • His books, in order of publication, include: With the Caravan (articles), 1952; Literary Questions (studies in literary criticism), 1956; The Iraqi Revolution (a study in modern history), 1985; Critical Studies in the Light of the Critical Method (literary criticism); Materialist Tendencies in Arab-Islamic Philosophy (a foundational work in the Marxist study of the Arab philosophical heritage, in two volumes), 1978; Studies in Islam (with Maḥmūd Amīn al-ʿĀlim, Muḥammad Dakrūb, and Samīr Saʿd), 1978; On Heritage and Islamic Law (studies), 1983; New Titles for Old Faces (studies on heritage and the thought of the Arab Renaissance), 1984; Our Heritage: How Should We Understand It? (studies on Arab heritage), 1986; and Studies in Thought and Literature (literary criticism, published after his assassination), 1993. He also left a large number of studies, research papers, and articles across many fields of knowledge. These were being collected and organized for publication in separate volumes.

  • Husayn Muruwwa was assassinated in his home on 17 February 1987. He was 79 years old.

    About forty years ago, virtually all we knew of al-Kindī came from reports preserved by historians and from incomplete excerpts of works whose full texts were unknown to us. This changed when the German Orientalist Ritter discovered a number of al-Kindī’s treatises in the Hagia Sophia Library in Istanbul and published them with the Orientalist Plessner in the Czechoslovak Orientalist journal in 1932. From then on, al-Kindī’s works began to appear in scholarly editions. Dr. Aḥmad Fuʾād al-Ahwānī in Cairo published Al-Kindī’s Book to al-Muʿtaṣim on First Philosophy in 1948. Muḥammad ʿAbd al-Hādī Abū Rīda, also in Cairo, published Al-Kindī’s Philosophical Treatises in two volumes containing twenty-five treatises between 1950 and 1953. Dr. Fayṣal Badawī in Iraq published Al-Kindī’s Treatise on the Making of Swords in 1962. Yūsuf Zakariyyā and Maḥmūd Aḥmad al-Ḥifnī worked with several Orientalists on scholarly editions of al-Kindī’s writings on music. Yūsuf Yaʿqūb Maskūnī in Baghdad published Al-Kindī’s Treatise on the Production of Weather. Orientalists including Ritter and Karl Garbers published al-Kindī’s work on the chemistry of perfume and sublimation, while Neheimer and others also took part in this work. Yet everything by al-Kindī that has so far been identified and published still represents only a very small part of the total body of work described by Ibn al-Nadīm, al-Qifṭī, Ibn Abī Uṣaybiʿa, and Qāḍī Ṣāʿid al-Andalusī. Ibn al-Nadīm lists 241 books and treatises by al-Kindī (The Fihrist, Leipzig, p. 255); Ibn Abī Uṣaybiʿa lists 281 (Classes of Physicians, Cairo, p. 29); and al-Qifṭī lists 228 (History of the Sages, Leipzig, p. 368). Qāḍī Ṣāʿid says that al-Kindī had more than fifty famous works in most branches of knowledge, ranging from long books to short treatises (Classes of Nations, Beirut, p. 52). What is actually available to readers today, however, amounts to no more than 42 printed works, 30 works still surviving in manuscript in libraries around the world, and 34 works translated into Latin, English, French, Italian, German, and Persian. Some of these translations survive even though their Arabic originals are lost. See Father Richard Joseph McCarthy, S.J., Works Attributed to the Philosopher of the Arabs, Baghdad, 1962.↩︎

    For al-Kindī, “rational knowledge” belongs to the human being’s “rational existence.” He divides human existence into sensory existence and rational existence, and he regards rational existence as the true form of existence. Sensory existence, by contrast, “is not stable, because what it encounters passes away, flows, and changes.” In al-Kindī’s system, rational existence is connected with universals, by which he means genera and species (previously cited source, pp. 84–85). The Platonic influence is obvious in his distinction between rational existence as “true” and sensory existence as “unstable.”↩︎

    In Arabic philosophical literature, Neoplatonism is called “the doctrine of the Alexandrians” because the school arose in Alexandria from the late first century BCE onward. Its influence continued into the period when Arabic philosophy began to develop.↩︎

  61. 61

    Plotinus (205–270 CE) was the second of the two principal figures of Neoplatonism. The first was Philo of Alexandria (25 BCE–40 CE), but it was Plotinus in the third century CE who brought the school to its fullest and most complete philosophical form. The only primary source for Plotinus’s philosophy is the Enneads, in which Porphyry of Tyre collected, organized, and classified the writings of his teacher Plotinus into six groups of nine treatises each—hence the title Enneads, or “Nines.” By the time Greek philosophy was translated into Arabic, parts of the final three Enneads had already been translated into Syriac under the title The Theology of Aristotle. The Arabs translated them into Arabic under the same title. This produced the famous historical confusion in which these texts were taken to be works of Aristotle, leading Arab philosophers to mix some of Aristotle’s ideas with those of Neoplatonism. We now have an Arabic translation of several chapters of the Enneads, published by Dr. ʿAbd al-Raḥmān Badawī in Plotinus among the Arabs. In 1970, an Arabic translation of the Fourth Ennead, On the Soul, was published by Fuʾād Zakariyyā and revised by Muḥammad Salīm Sālim (Ministry of Culture, Egypt).↩︎

    Aristotle defines the soul as “the first actuality of a natural, organized body capable of life” (2, 412b 5). In Aristotle, form plays the role of actuality—or completion—in relation to matter, which remains only potentially existent until form brings its existence into actuality (Aristotle, 12, 1069b 34). Richard Walzer supports our view that when al-Kindī speaks of the soul as “form,” he means the term in Aristotle’s sense. Walzer says that al-Kindī “refers to Aristotle’s definition of the soul as the form of the body or the completion of the body” (Walzer, Islamic Philosophy and Its Place in Human Thought, trans. Tawfīq Ḥusayn, p. 41).↩︎

    We think that the treatises addressed to unnamed individuals were probably written to al-Kindī’s students, for two reasons. First, the openings use the tone of a teacher addressing someone who has asked him for knowledge. At the start of the Treatise on the Intellect, for example, al-Kindī says: “I understood what you asked me to set down concerning my account of the intellect” (Al-Kindī’s Philosophical Treatises, vol. 1, p. 353). Second, al-Kindī uses the same tone in two treatises that explicitly name men known to have been his students. One is Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad al-Khurāsānī; see al-Kindī’s Treatise Explaining the Finitude of the Body of the World, Al-Kindī’s Philosophical Treatises, vol. 1, p. 185; and Father McCarthy, p. 63, no. 111. Ibn al-Nadīm (The Fihrist, p. 261) says that this man was better known as Aḥmad ibn al-Ṭayyib, that he studied under al-Kindī and learned from him, that he later taught the caliph al-Muʿtaḍid (279–289 AH/892–901 CE), and that he was killed in 286 AH/899 CE; see Ibn Abī Uṣaybiʿa, Classes of Physicians, vol. 1, p. 214. The second student whom al-Kindī names is ʿAlī ibn al-Jahm; see Al-Kindī’s Treatise to ʿAlī ibn al-Jahm on the Oneness of God and the Finitude of the Body of the World, Al-Kindī’s Philosophical Treatises, vol. 1, p. 201; and Father McCarthy, p. 48, no. 291. This ʿAlī ibn al-Jahm is the well-known Abbasid poet who praised the caliph al-Mutawakkil, was exiled by him in 232 AH, and died in 249 AH. The sources name other students of al-Kindī as well, including Ḥasanawayh, Nafṭawayh, Salmawayh, Abū Isḥāq Ibrāhīm Quwayrī, and Ibn Karnīb. See Ibn al-Nadīm, The Fihrist, p. 412; and al-Ahwānī, Al-Kindī, Philosopher of the Arabs, p. 77.↩︎

I understood what you asked me to set down concerning the intellect: a brief account of my view, following the opinion of the most highly regarded of the ancient Greeks, foremost among them Aristotle and his teacher, the sage Plato, since Plato’s position on this matter amounted to the position of his pupil Aristotle.” As this passage clearly shows, al-Kindī states that Plato and Aristotle agree in their theory of the intellect. On that basis, he then goes on to present Aristotle’s theory rather than Plato’s, despite the difference between the two theories.↩︎

    The section of this treatise dealing with universals, species, and the rational soul can be found in Al-Kindī’s Philosophical Treatises, vol. 1, p. 155, or in al-Ahwānī’s edition of Al-Kindī’s Book to al-Muʿtaṣim, p. 134. The passage reads: “The soul becomes actually intelligent when the species unite with it; before they unite with it, it is intelligent only potentially. Anything that exists potentially is brought into actuality by something else that is itself actual in the respect in which it brings the other from potentiality to actuality. What brings the soul, which is potentially intelligent, into actual intelligence is the union with it of the species and genera of things—that is, their universals, and these are the universals of their individual realities [this is the reading in al-Ahwānī’s edition; Abū Rīda’s edition reads: ‘Are universals their individual realities?’]. Through their union with the soul, the soul becomes intelligent—that is, it possesses an intellect, namely the universals of things. The universals of things, when present in the soul and brought from potentiality into actuality, are the soul’s acquired intellect, which it possessed only potentially, through the actual intellect that brought the soul from potentiality into actuality. Since universals are many, intellect is many....”↩︎

  134. 134

    The three kinds of intellect that can be drawn from Aristotle’s discussion in On the Soul are: 1. an intellect whose nature is to make all things actual—the active intellect; 2. an intellect that becomes all things—the potential intellect; and 3. the habitual intellect, the human intellect when it is actual. Aristotle illustrates this last state with the example of a learned person who has acquired knowledge and can use it immediately whenever he wishes. This kind of intellect therefore stands between potentiality and actuality: it is actual because the person truly possesses the knowledge, but potential because at a given moment he may not be actively using it. See Aristotle, 3, 430a 10–19; 430a 16; 429b 1–5. Alexander of Aphrodisias, one of the leading commentators on Aristotle between the second and third centuries CE, also divided intellect into three kinds: 1. the material intellect (intellectus materialis), which is intellect in potentiality; 2. an intellect that understands—that is, an actual intellect possessing a settled capacity for understanding (intellectus qui intelligit et habet habitum ut intelligat), so that it can exercise this ability whenever it wishes; and 3. the active intellect (intelligentia agens), an external agent that gives intelligibility to the human intellect and to intelligible forms. Its relation to the potential intellect in the soul is like the relation of light to the eye. In Alexander’s view, this active intellect is necessary for the union of the material intellect with the intelligible form, bringing the intellect from potentiality into actuality. A section of Alexander of Aphrodisias’s On the Soul was translated into Latin as a separate treatise entitled De intellectu et intellecto (“On the Intellect and the Intelligible”). See Muḥammad ʿAbd al-Hādī Abū Rīda, introduction to al-Kindī’s Treatise on the Intellect, in Al-Kindī’s Philosophical Treatises, vol. 1, pp. 320–321.↩︎

  139. 139

    Aristotle devotes chapters 4 and 5 of Book XIII of the Metaphysics to discussing Plato’s theory of Forms. If we look especially at the discussion in chapter 5, we can see that Aristotle rejects separating the universal, which can be grasped by the intellect, from the sensory world. He also rejects a metaphysical separation—in the sense opposed to a dialectical one—between essence and appearance. And he rejects treating the universal as independent of the particular, as though the universal could exist outside particular things. From these aspects of Aristotle’s criticism of Plato’s theory of Forms, Lenin drew the conclusion expressed in his Philosophical Notebooks: Aristotle’s criticism is directed not only against Plato, but against idealism in general.↩︎

  141. 141

    Aristotle may appear to be a sensualist when he stresses this point. But he distances himself from sensualism in On the Soul (2, 417b 22), where he makes clear that although knowledge begins with the senses, it is not formed from sensation and experience alone. He says that science is knowledge of the universal, not the particular, while actual sense perception deals only with individual things—the particulars—and “science concerns the universal.” Here we have used the Arabic text of On the Soul, translated by Isḥāq ibn Ḥunayn, Badawī ed., p. 43. In the Philosophical Notebooks, Lenin likewise rejected the charge of “sensualism” against Aristotle, calling him a thoughtful sensualist in contrast to crude sensualists.↩︎

    See al-Kindī’s Treatise Explaining the Proximate Efficient Cause of Generation and Corruption (Al-Kindī’s Philosophical Treatises, vol. 1, pp. 214–237). In this treatise he builds his logical arguments on the assumption that what a proximate cause does is a real, actual, tangible event, not something merely figurative. He says, for example, that motion produces heat in the elements and in things composed of them, and that the elements are affected by motion or by contact. Here motion is an efficient cause of heat. Motion is a real material fact, and heat is a real material fact. The first causes the second, and the cause itself is therefore real and material. What sense, then, does it make to call it merely a figurative cause?↩︎

  193. 193

    The ideological character of philosophy—of every philosophy—is an objective fact. It does not depend on whether the philosopher is aware of it, nor on whether we recognize it in one philosopher or another. Like every other form of human consciousness, philosophy has no history separate from the history of real people living under particular economic and social conditions. In every society and every age, philosophy therefore presents a system of ideas about the world in which the character of the prevailing social relations and the ideological struggle within those relations are indirectly reflected. Through these ideas, philosophy also defines each philosopher’s position within that struggle.↩︎

  194. 194

    Medieval Arab philosophers knew the work called Theology as The Theology of Aristotle or Aristotle’s Book of Divinity. The mistaken attribution to Aristotle may have arisen because the work, whose author was then unknown, reached them together with explanations by Porphyry of Tyre, whom they knew as a commentator on Aristotle. They therefore assumed that the work itself was by Aristotle. ʿAbd al-Masīḥ ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Nāʿima al-Ḥimṣī (d. 220 AH/835 CE) translated it into Arabic, and al-Kindī revised the translation. Dieterici first published it in Berlin in 1882, and it was translated into Latin in 1519. In reality, the work is drawn from the Fourth and Sixth Enneads of Plotinus. See ʿAbd al-Raḥmān Badawī’s edition of the Fourth Ennead, On the Soul, Cairo, 1970, pp. 156–157.↩︎

  203. 203

    Al-Fārābī contradicts himself on this point. His entire philosophical system is built on emanation, which necessarily rules out creation from nothing and implies the eternity of the world; this is also what the meaning of his philosophical texts themselves requires. Yet in The Harmonization of the Opinions of the Two Sages (same edition, pp. 100–104), he says that God brought the world into existence from nothing (pp. 101, 103, 104), and that the world came into being. He even calls the belief that Aristotle held the world to be eternal “an ugly and objectionable supposition” (p. 100). How should we understand this contradiction, and which of al-Fārābī’s two positions should we accept? In our view, the contradiction is apparent rather than real. It was a means of self-protection—a method Arab-Islamic philosophers of the period allowed themselves to use to an unreasonable degree. Their real views are those embodied in their philosophical theories, not the statements they make outside those theories. Otherwise their entire philosophical systems would become meaningless.↩︎

    Ibid., p. 74. It should be noted that al-Fārābī understands the relation between matter and form in existing things in the Aristotelian way. When a particular form belongs to a particular matter, the form is not always absolutely form, nor is the matter always absolutely matter. A form can be form in relation to what lies below it and matter in relation to what lies above it. In the same way, matter can be matter in relation to what lies above it and form in relation to what lies below it. In the present case, al-Fārābī says that the imaginative faculty is matter in relation to what stands above it, namely the rational faculty. The rational faculty, in turn, is form in relation to the imaginative faculty because it stands above it. The rational faculty remains form, since no faculty of the soul stands above it. This is what he means when he says: “It is the form of every form that comes before it.” Elsewhere he says that the rational faculty governs the imaginative faculty and the chief sensory faculty—that is, the other faculties of the soul (p. 72). In another passage (p. 70), he says that the rational faculty is what allows us to grasp intelligible things, distinguish ugly from beautiful, and acquire crafts and sciences.↩︎

  216. 216

    We should point out that al-Fārābī and the other Arab philosophers who represent the rationalist current, like the Muslim theologians and Sufis, all begin from the principle of God’s oneness understood in terms of absolute transcendence. This is the fixed starting point they all share. Their differences lie in how they deal with the contradiction that arises between absolute transcendence and the ideological positions that force them to seek some connection between God and the world. In our view, this effort expressed their opposition to the theoretical foundation of the official ideology: the absolute separation of God from the world, which in reality reflected the principle of absolute separation between one human being and another—that is, between ruler and ruled. As we saw earlier, the Sufis establish a direct link between the world and God through unveiling and direct vision. The rationalist philosophers, by contrast, establish this link through intermediaries. The theory of emanation gave them the basis for these intermediaries—the separate intellects.↩︎

  225. 225

    He means the first matter common to the whole natural world. Al-Fārābī’s insistence on a “common nature” shared by the celestial bodies, on a common first matter, and on an existential relation between the two points toward a view of the world as a unity. His texts on this subject suggest that he tends to ground this unity materially. In none of these passages does he refer to “essence.” Instead, he repeatedly speaks of a common “matter” passing through the celestial world in a “process” that produces the “matter” of the natural world. This matter is itself common and moves on its own within natural things through another “process” that raises them gradually from lower to higher forms “until each species reaches the highest perfection of its substance.”↩︎

  226. 226

    Although the Aristotelian account of the relation between “form and matter” is idealist because it separates matter’s form from matter itself, its content in al-Fārābī comes closer to materialism. He describes the relation in a way that makes it appear as an internal process within the movement of matter itself.↩︎

  227. 227

    One might ask: how can this relation work independently of every external factor when al-Fārābī ultimately traces the existence of natural things back to the celestial bodies? Our answer has two parts. First, the text we are discussing explicitly says that natural motion in existing things operates according to its own internal laws and is genuinely independent of any external factor. Second, all of al-Fārābī’s texts on the celestial bodies and the emergence of natural beings from them indicate that matter exists throughout the celestial world, that a moving “process” takes place within this celestial world—which is itself bodily—and that this process passes through stages on its way toward natural existence in our earthly world. In the chain of emanation, the first intellect necessarily brings with it the existence of the first heaven, which is material. Each following intellect in turn entails the existence of another heaven, or celestial body, down to the sphere of the moon. We also find that, in al-Fārābī’s system, the celestial bodies “are of the same kind as hylomorphic [material-natural] beings, in that they have subjects resembling the matters prepared to receive forms, and they have things like forms through which they become substances, with those things existing in those subjects” (The Virtuous City, pp. 52–53). There is therefore a material link between the celestial world and the natural world. If we also take into account the eternal character of the whole system of emanation, and al-Fārābī’s statement that the celestial bodies share with the ten intellects the fact that from the very beginning they were given the best state in which they could exist as substances, along with their quantities, shapes, and visible qualities (p. 54), we can conclude that matter is eternal. From eternity it has been moving within a continuous process of its own, passing from one stage to another until the natural world comes into existence, where the process continues in new forms. In other words, al-Fārābī does not speak of matter existing apart from nature, nor does he speak here of an essence. He speaks of real matter.↩︎

A single thing therefore cannot remain forever numerically one; instead, its permanence through time is made a permanence of species. For a species to remain one, individuals of that species must exist for a time, then perish and be replaced by other individuals of the same species. This continues in the same way without end” (The Virtuous City, pp. 63–64).↩︎

Whoever wants the truth without hesitation should seek that other book. Whoever wants the truth presented in a way that gives some consideration to our colleagues, with fuller explanation and hints which, if properly understood, make the other book unnecessary, should use this book [that is, The Healing].” See ʿAbd al-Raḥmān Badawī, The Greek Heritage in Islamic Civilization, 3rd ed., p. 277, quoting a copy in the Cairo University Library, nos. 26050–26053, itself taken from a British Museum manuscript, fol. 3b, lines 3–6.↩︎

  272. 272

    Aristotelian demonstration has a scientific character. Aristotle, however, does not explain the scientific or certain character of a demonstration by its conformity to formal syllogistic rules. He grounds it instead in whether the causal structure contained in the demonstration corresponds to reality. He therefore holds that each kind of being requires its own form of demonstration, suited to that kind of being, because demonstration always has an ontological side. Each type of existence, in his view, opens a particular path by which the researcher can discover what that type of existence contains.↩︎

  285. 285

    On the basis of this conclusion, al-Fārābī is ahead of Descartes on the question of knowledge, especially our knowledge of first rational principles, or axioms. Descartes traces our knowledge of axioms back to reason itself. For him, knowledge begins with intuition: the mind recognizes axioms that, he says, are already present in the human soul. They do not arise from repeated experience of the external world. God places them in the human mind at birth, and reason later grasps them by itself without sensory knowledge.↩︎

  289. 289

    It should be remembered that by “Peripatetics,” al-Sabzawārī means the Arab-Islamic philosophers, including al-Fārābī. We do not, however, agree with the common practice of calling the Arab philosophers “Peripatetics” without qualification. They were not all equally close to Aristotle’s philosophy. Even those most closely connected with it, such as Ibn Rushd, did not agree with Aristotle in all or even most of their views. Al-Fārābī departs from Peripatetic philosophy more than any of them. And how can they simply be called “Peripatetics” when their connection with Neoplatonism is so obvious?↩︎

  291. 291

    The way of knowing that al-Fārābī describes here also appears in statements such as “universals [essences] are obtained from particulars” and “universals are, in truth, experiences.” This approach can be seen as an example of Lenin’s statement that the “essence of things” or their “substance” expresses nothing more than human knowledge of things—a knowledge that continuously deepens—and of his statement that essences are relative rather than fixed properties of things (Lenin, Materialism and Empirio-Criticism, Arabic ed., trans. Munīr Mashāyiḵ, Damascus, 1971, p. 263).↩︎

  292. 292

    Al-Fārābī’s understanding of the relation between sensory and rational knowledge, as we have explained it, can be seen as an early form of understanding the dialectical relation between essence and appearance. As we see it, he was able, even if spontaneously, to approach the dialectical-materialist proposition that the senses reflect external appearances and particulars in sensory images, while the essence of phenomena cannot be grasped by the senses alone. The internal unity between a phenomenon and its essence is what makes the transition from sensory to rational knowledge possible.↩︎

  293. 293

    His name was al-Ḥusayn, his kunya was Abū ʿAlī, and in Arabic philosophical literature he is known by the title “the Supreme Master” (al-Shaykh al-Raʾīs). He was born in 370 AH/980 CE in the village of Afshana near Bukhara. He spent his early childhood in the town of Kharmaythan, also in the Bukhara region, where his father, ʿAbd Allāh ibn Sīnā, served as administrator on behalf of the Samanid ruler Nūḥ ibn Manṣūr. In Bukhara itself, Ibn Sīnā studied with private tutors in his father’s home and later continued learning through his own efforts. He tells us this in the autobiography that he partly dictated to his student Abū ʿUbayd al-Jūzjānī, who completed the account after his teacher’s death. The biography is reproduced by al-Qifṭī in Informing the Scholars of the Lives of the Sages, p. 269, and by Ibn Abī Uṣaybiʿa in Classes of Physicians, vol. 2, p. 2, where Ibn Abī Uṣaybiʿa gives Ibn Sīnā’s birth year as 375 AH. Ibn Sīnā died in Hamadan, Iran, in 428 AH/1036 CE.↩︎

  294. 294

    In Ibn Sīnā’s time, the Arab caliphate had reached an advanced stage of division and fragmentation. During the fifty-eight years of his life, the “Supreme Master” lived while three Islamic caliphates existed at the same time: the Abbasid caliphate in the East (132–656 AH/750–1258 CE), the Fatimid caliphate in Egypt and North Africa (297–567 AH/909–1171 CE), and the Umayyad caliphate in al-Andalus (300–407 AH/912–1016 CE). Alongside these caliphates were several Islamic states linked only formally to the Abbasid caliphate: the Samanid state, with its capital at Bukhara (261–389 AH/874–998 CE); the Buyid state in Fars, Rayy, Hamadan, Isfahan, and Iraq (320–447 AH/932–1055 CE); and the Ghaznavid state, with its capital at Ghazna in Afghanistan (351–582 AH/962–1186 CE). There were also the small ṭāʾifa states in the Maghreb and breakaway principalities within these larger states, such as the principality of ʿAlāʾ al-Dīn ibn Kākawayh, a former Buyid military commander who seized Hamadan and Isfahan in 414 AH/1023 CE. Ibn Sīnā also lived through the final period of the Hamdanid emirate of Aleppo (333–394 AH/944–1002 CE).↩︎

In Dialectics of Nature, Engels says that Bacon’s empiricism became the starting point of modern metaphysics, which separates phenomena from one another without attending to the connections between them.     There is abundant evidence for this in Ibn Sīnā, and it shows that sensory knowledge must rely on reasoning, while reasoning must also rely on sensory knowledge. In The Salvation (p. 65), for example, he says that the senses grasp particulars, while rational thought reaches abstract universals. In the chapter on sensory data (The Salvation, p. 61), he says that matters established by experience—meaning sensory experience—are propositions to which the senses lead us with the help of reasoning. In defining induction, he says that it is “a judgment about a universal because that judgment is found in the particulars belonging to that universal, either in all of them, which is complete induction, or in most of them, which is the commonly used form of induction” (The Salvation, p. 58). See also Pointers and Reminders, vol. 3, pp. 17–19, where Ibn Sīnā answers those who claim that only what can be sensed truly exists.↩︎

    Ibn Sīnā uses this name in States of the Soul, p. 61, and in The Salvation, p. 163. In Pointers and Reminders, vol. 2, p. 353, he writes it as bifṭāsiyā. The word is Greek in origin: phantasia. Aristotle used it in the sense of imagination and says that the word is derived from “light” (phaos). See Aristotle, On the Soul, Arabic ed., trans. al-Ahwānī, 2nd ed., Cairo, 1962, p. 107. Here Aristotle and Ibn Sīnā differ both in terminology and in substance. Aristotle uses phantasia for the imaginative faculty and treats it as the second stage in the process of thinking, with common sense as the first. Ibn Sīnā, by contrast, applies phantasia to common sense itself, even though he explains the word as meaning imagination. They also differ in how they explain common sense. Ibn Sīnā says that it is the faculty that receives all the forms impressed upon the senses. Aristotle says that common sense perceives motion, rest, shape, magnitude, number, and unity—things that no single sense perceives on its own. See same source, pp. 93–101.↩︎

    Ibid. We should also note the bodily organs in the brain that Ibn Sīnā assigns to each of these powers of internal sensory perception. In Pointers and Reminders (vol. 2, pp. 353–355), he calls these bodily organs “instruments,” and sometimes refers to them as the “seat” of perception. In The Salvation, he simply gives the place “assigned” in the brain to each faculty. Common sense is “a faculty located in the first cavity of the brain”; the image-preserving faculty is “located at the back of the front cavity of the brain”; the imaginative faculty is “located in the middle cavity of the brain”; the estimative faculty is “located at the rear of the middle cavity of the brain”; and the retaining or memory faculty is “located in the rear cavity of the brain.” These locations naturally reflect the level of scientific knowledge of brain anatomy in the medieval Arab period. Philosophically, however, they also show an advanced tendency to connect the process of thought with the brain’s physical organs, which here points toward a materialist outlook. Modern science identifies the brain’s gray matter, especially the cerebral cortex, as one of the main physical organs involved in cognition.↩︎

    We should quote the following passage because it clearly shows Ibn Sīnā’s method in his theory of universals. He says: “Universals, and the judgments and concepts that concern them, are not grasped by the senses or imagination, nor are they themselves objects of intuition or experience. But the senses and imagination assist the intellect. As for forming concepts: the senses present mixed things to the imagination, the imagination presents them to the intellect, and the intellect then separates, distinguishes, and divides them. It takes each meaning on its own and arranges what is more particular and more general, what belongs to the essence and what is accidental. In this way the first meanings needed for concepts become present in the intellect, and it then combines them into definitions. As for judgments, the senses and imagination may assist [the intellect] through experience or intuition, and they may assist it through induction.... They may also assist indirectly: first by helping to supply the concepts, after which the concepts are combined through affirmation and negation. The intellect then sees what must be accepted as self-evident, and it sees the syllogism by which other judgments must be acquired.” The Salvation, pp. 65–66. This passage gives a detailed account of how the intellect moves from sensory experience to the universal. It confirms that, in Ibn Sīnā’s theory of universals, the intellect depends on sensory experience. Intuition is mentioned here only incidentally. We will return to this later.↩︎

    Modern scholars disagree about the intellectual relationship between Pointers and Reminders and Ibn Sīnā’s earlier works, especially The Healing and The Salvation. Some argue that when Ibn Sīnā wrote Pointers and Reminders, as well as his symbolic stories—The Treatise of the Bird, Ḥayy ibn Yaqẓān, Salāmān and Absāl, and The Treatise on Love—he moved away from the Peripatetic ideas that stand out in The Healing and finally turned toward a Sufi form of illuminationist wisdom. This view is represented, for example, by L. Gardet in his article on the religious idea in Ibn Sīnā, published in Revue du Caire, June 1951, and by Sulaymān Dunyā in the introduction to his Cairo 1947 edition of Pointers and Reminders. Other scholars deny that The Healing and Ibn Sīnā’s other early works ceased to express his real views. This is the position of scholars such as Carra de Vaux, Avicenna, Arabic ed., p. 150, and the French Orientalist A. M. Goichon in The Philosophy of Ibn Sīnā, Arabic ed., Beirut, 1950, p. 18. We accept this second view. We have found nothing in Pointers and Reminders that Ibn Sīnā had not already said in his other works. The book differs mainly in two ways. The first is formal: the way it is composed, the material is arranged, and the discussion is divided into sections. The second concerns expression: the style used to present the ideas and the beauty of the language. The writing is more concentrated and compressed, and in the later chapters Ibn Sīnā sometimes uses symbols and sometimes interprets the outward wording of Qurʾānic passages. These stylistic features may be what idealist scholars used to support the claim that Ibn Sīnā changed the positions expressed in his earlier works, where some materialist tendencies are visible, and ended by adopting an illuminationist-Sufi outlook. Some of these scholars also appeal to remarks in the introduction to a work published under Ibn Sīnā’s name as The Logic of the Easterners (Cairo, 1910), where he appears to disagree with the Peripatetics. They also use Ibn Ṭufayl’s statement in the introduction to Ḥayy ibn Yaqẓān that Ibn Sīnā said at the beginning of The Healing that the truth as he understood it was different from what that book contained. See Ibn Ṭufayl, Ḥayy ibn Yaqẓān, Dār al-Maʿārif ed., Beirut, 1954, p. 8. In reality, even in The Healing, Ibn Sīnā does not agree completely with Aristotle or with Peripatetic philosophy in general. He differs from them on many points and alters many positions. As for the special section of Pointers and Reminders on the “Stations of the Knowers,” first, it is a mixture of ideas scattered through his other books; and second, it is a descriptive discussion, not a reflection of Ibn Sīnā’s own way of life, as we know from his historically well-established biography.↩︎

    The Qurʾānic passage in question is: “God is the light of the heavens and the earth. The likeness of His light is as a niche containing a lamp; the lamp is in a glass; the glass is like a shining star, lit from a blessed olive tree, neither eastern nor western, whose oil would almost glow even if no fire touched it—light upon light...” (Qurʾān 24:35). Ibn Sīnā applies this verse to the levels of intellect in his own theory. He interprets the “niche” as the material intellect; the “olive tree” as the thinking faculty—that is, rational reflection assisted by sensory perceptions; the “oil” as intuition, through which knowledge is gained without discursive thought; the “glass” as the habitual intellect; the phrase “whose oil would almost glow even if no fire touched it” as the highest degree of intuition, which he calls the holy faculty; and “light upon light” as the stage of perfection reached when the intellect becomes an acquired intellect. He interprets the “lamp” as the rational faculty once it becomes an actual intellect: the human soul can then “bring before itself, whenever it wishes, an intelligible already acquired and completed as though it were directly present, without needing to acquire it again” (Pointers and Reminders, vol. 2, pp. 369–376). Al-Ghazālī, however, reverses the relation and treats the Qurʾānic verse as an interpretation of these levels of theoretical intellect. See al-Ghazālī, The Niche of Lights, p. 58.↩︎

    In logic, the middle term is the universal proposition relied on in a syllogism to move from what is known to what is unknown—that is, from the minor premise to the required conclusion. This universal proposition, which functions as the middle term, may come either from first rational principles, or axioms, or from theoretical propositions derived from the particulars of external reality.     The question of how consciousness arises in the brain remained unclear to scientists until the famous Soviet scientist Pavlov explained it in the way we described earlier. Before Marx, this question remained a puzzle even for materialist philosophers. Like the idealists, some materialists would say either that consciousness is an essence completely independent of matter, so that body and consciousness work separately but in parallel by some kind of miracle, or they would give a crude explanation and say that the brain secretes thought just as the mouth secretes saliva—that thought simply flows from it automatically. Lenin criticized this crude view, arguing that explaining thought as matter is just as false as explaining matter as thought, because vulgar materialism quickly slips into idealism.↩︎

One might object that this statement, the one before it, and the earlier examples we cited of the intellect forming universals from particulars—as in the case of an eclipse—occur in Ibn Sīnā’s discussion of divine matters, or metaphysics, and therefore do not apply to the material world. Our answer is twofold. First, Ibn Sīnā uses ideas of this kind in that context because he treats them as general principles already accepted in the particular sciences, such as natural science and mathematics. He then uses them as grounds for his views in “divine science.” Second, we do not separate a philosopher’s ideas in metaphysics from his ideas in other fields. All of them come from a single source: the real world reflected in his thought in one form or another. His metaphysical ideas are simply one form of that reflection. They are particular echoes of the way he relates to the real world and of his particular position in society.↩︎

    Aristotle sees the relation of matter to form as similar to the relation of the individual to the universal that includes it and other individuals. Form, in other words, is the concept or essence in relation to matter. Callias and Socrates, Aristotle’s example, are the same in species but differ from one another in their matter (Aristotle, Metaphysics, 7, 1034a 5 ff.). Ibn Sīnā, by contrast, treats matter as the underlying “subject” in relation to form, and this subject is a substance. “Subject” and “substance” are not the same as essence. See The Salvation, p. 200; and al-Shahrastānī, Religions and Sects, vol. 2, p. 74. We will explain this point in detail in the discussion that follows.↩︎

  457. 457

    Aristotle’s dualism of matter and form appears in two ways. First, he treats matter as merely receptive and passive, while form alone is active and acts upon matter. He does not recognize the dialectical unity of mutual influence between them in the way Ibn Sīnā does. See Aristotle, Metaphysics, 7, 1029a 19. Second, matter itself has a double character in Aristotle’s view. Matter is potentiality in relation to form, while form is the actual realization of that potentiality. Matter is therefore pure possibility on one side, and an actual reality realized through form on the other. In this sense it becomes relative: a thing is matter—that is, existence—from one point of view, and form—that is, concept—from another. Matter in itself is therefore not treated as something definite in relation to form. See Aristotle, same source, 7, 1041a–b 5–6. We will see in the course of the discussion how Ibn Sīnā overcame this problem partly, if not completely.↩︎

  459. 459

    In ancient and then medieval philosophy, the term “divine science” meant philosophy of existence in its broadest sense—universal being as a whole. It was the main branch of ancient philosophy, which is why Aristotle called it “first philosophy.” Philosophy at that time included all the sciences and was even called “the science of sciences.” Sciences that dealt with particular kinds of existence, such as natural science, mathematics, and social science, were called particular sciences. For this reason, when Ibn Sīnā speaks of “divine science” in this older sense, we treat him as speaking about philosophy, and we treat the principles of that science as the principles of philosophy itself.↩︎

    Alongside the many examples already mentioned and others that will appear later, we can give one concrete example here. It occurs in The Salvation (pp. 236–237) in the proof of the Necessary Existent, within the “divine” section of Ibn Sīnā’s philosophy. In arguing that “there must be something that necessarily exists,” Ibn Sīnā uses a proof by division in the Platonic manner. When his divisions of possible existence reach the possibility of something coming into being and then ceasing to exist immediately, with no interval of time—in other words, coming to be and passing away at the same instant—he says this is impossible “because instants do not follow one another [as discrete units], and for numerically distinct individuals to come into existence one after another without the continuity found in something like motion would require instants [times] to follow one another, and natural science has already shown this to be impossible....” Ibn Sīnā is therefore using a law of natural science as part of a proof in “divine science.” This is a concrete example of how he relies on theoretical generalizations drawn from the study of nature in arguments concerning the metaphysical world.↩︎

    Ibn Sīnā does not picture the “first mover” as motionless in the way Aristotle does. He speaks clearly and explicitly on this point: “A mover implies something moved. But this implication does not mean that the moved thing must be something other than the mover, or that it must be the mover itself. (...) We therefore did not rule out the possibility of conceiving something that moves itself until a proof establishes that this is impossible. The mere concepts of mover and moved do not themselves rule it out. A moved thing requires something from which its motion comes, without requiring that this be either another thing or itself; and a mover requires something moved by it, without requiring that this be either another thing or itself....” The Salvation, p. 244.↩︎

An eternal existent, therefore, is not called an effect because, as he says in the passage quoted above, “non-existence did not precede it.” This confirms that Ibn Sīnā deliberately rejects the relation of acting, agency, and being acted upon between the first cause and its effect, the world, because this effect is as eternal as its cause.↩︎

    Another piece of evidence for the eternity of time in Ibn Sīnā is his statement: “Time is not brought into existence through a temporal coming-to-be. Time is therefore originated—that is, its Creator [originator] precedes it only....” The passage goes on to say that motion, like time, also does not come into being through a temporal beginning. He may not have taken account of Ibn Sīnā’s doctrine of “origination,” on which the idea of “originated” time rests. Ibn Sīnā’s purpose in this doctrine is precisely to affirm the eternity of what is originated in this sense, whether matter, motion, or time.↩︎

    Ibn Sīnā regards matter as a substance. Among his statements to this effect is: “Accidents come after matter by nature (...), while matter and form come before accidents by nature and causally” (The Salvation, p. 99). By contrast, he denies that motion is a substance. For example, he says: “Every motion is something that can increase and decrease, while no substance is like that. Therefore no motion is a substance” (The Salvation, p. 105). The basis of this denial is clear: substance is treated as static, while motion consists precisely in change and instability, since it can increase and decrease. Substance, on this view, is fixed and does not admit increase, decrease, transformation, or opposites in itself.↩︎

    Although Ibn Sīnā is generally known to question whether motion occurs in the categories of quality and quantity, here he says that it does occur in both, just as it occurs in the categories of place and position. He limits motion in quality to qualities that can become weaker or more intense, such as whiteness and blackness. As for position, he says that in his own view it does admit motion: the rotation of a round body around itself. We find no motion in the category of time, because matter has time only through motion itself. See The Salvation, pp. 101–107.↩︎

Dividing existence into substances and accidents points to an attempt to distinguish what is basic and stable from what is accidental, or to distinguish the content that gives a phenomenon its particular nature from what is external or merely formal, however necessary it may be.↩︎

    Al-Fārābī, The Opinions of the People of the Virtuous City, ed. Nādir, Beirut, 1959, p. 44. Al-Fārābī makes the multiplicity within the separate intellect twofold, while Ibn Sīnā makes it threefold. Al-Fārābī’s twofold scheme works as follows: from the First, God, there proceeds a first intellect. Insofar as this intellect thinks its principle, God, a second intellect proceeds from it; insofar as it thinks itself, the “first heaven” proceeds from it. The same pattern continues through the remaining intellects. From each intellect in sequence, in addition to the next intellect, there also proceeds a star or a celestial sphere. These spheres arise in the following order: the sphere of the fixed stars, Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, the Sun, Venus, Mercury, and the Moon.↩︎

    Ibn Sīnā expresses his view of circular motion as the basis of the different forms of motion in several ways. In the Nayrūziyya Treatise, he divides the natural sciences into the ethereal and the elemental. He says that the first is characterized by circular motion, while the second is characterized by a readiness for different forms of motion. See the Nayrūziyya Treatise, in Ibn Sīnā, Treatises on Wisdom and Natural Philosophy, Istanbul, 1298 AH, p. 93. In The Salvation (p. 138), he says that simple bodies are by nature capable of losing their particular position and place. Anything with this capacity must necessarily contain a principle of circular motion. This statement applies to all bodies. Simple bodies differ only in that the loss of position and place exists in them potentially by nature, while in other bodies it exists actually. Every body therefore necessarily contains a principle of some circular motion. Among compound bodies, some move in circles, while others move in straight lines; most compound bodies belong to the second group.↩︎

    Ibn Sīnā also argues that earthly natural bodies contain within themselves an inclination toward straight-line motion. See Pointers and Reminders, vol. 2, pp. 216–219. More generally, Ibn Sīnā recognized several forms of motion, much as Francis Bacon (1561–1626), with whom the age of modern philosophy begins, would do about six centuries later. Bacon spoke of the motion of fire, air, water, expansion, and contraction. Similar forms appear in Ibn Sīnā as well. It is clear, however, that Ibn Sīnā ultimately reduces all forms of motion to motion in place.↩︎

  559. 559

    Ibn Sīnā gives another account of the idea we mean here. He imagines that behind every motion there is an inclination or moving power, and that each segment of motion is driven by a new inclination or a new power. At the end of each segment, the first inclination comes to an end once it has carried the motion to its limit, so the next segment requires another inclination. Between the two successive inclinations—or the two successive segments of motion—there is rest. Every straight motion is therefore followed by rest, as is every motion across a finite distance. Two motions do not continue directly into one another (The Salvation, pp. 139–140). This brings Ibn Sīnā close to the idea that motion in matter contains a unity of discontinuity and continuity, as we noted earlier. In dialectical materialism, this means the unity of motion and rest: rest is only one stage within motion.↩︎
